evidence: task/instruction.md is 116 words in three short paragraphs, first person throughout, with a contraction and a personal working habit rather than a feature list: line 1 "I'd like a small local playground for working on JavaScript and complete HTML files. The editor itself matters: I often paste a long one-line experiment, format it, make changes in several places, and then run it beside the source. I want to keep the versions that work without losing a draft when another tab saves first."; line 5 "I should be able to open it, edit code, run it and inspect the result without signing in." Sentence length varies (5 to 30 words); there are no bullets, headings, numbered lists, em dashes or marketing gloss. A pattern scan of instruction.md and all six notes for seamless/robust/delve/leverage/intuitive/ensure/comprehensive/streamline/furthermore/moreover/additionally found zero hits, and zero bullet or numbered list lines in any of the seven files. The skill's cross-file test (a voice that changes between instruction.md and the notes) is met in kind: the notes stay in the same first-person owner voice, e.g. overview.md "stays current in each of them while I work", ui.md "as long as the source I see is drawn by your own surface" and "for as long as I keep typing at those carets, however slowly", integration.md heading "How I start the app" and "I start it with node /app/server.js", with contractions in ui.md ("Don't use a textarea"). NOTE (not a defect): the notes are much denser and more imperative than the brief (about 1,900 words; 'must' occurs in every note; long precise sentences such as the overview.md console-error sentence), so the register is closer to a careful written spec than to casual speech, and first-person markers are sparse in policy.md and security.md. That is the expected role of note files and the person's voice is still present, so it does not reach the skill's defect bar of uniform cadence, gloss or parallel bullets. NOTE: line 3 "Please read the six notes in /instructions before building. They describe the custom editor, preview, saved snippets and runtime." is the most template-like sentence in the brief, but it is plain and short. This row is a prose judgement; no runtime evidence is required for it and none is claimed.
